drapeaux.note: Summary of figures from the HRW report (published in English); translated from the French entry, not re-copied verbatim from the report.

titre: Rwanda's Gacaca: A Customary Name for a State Court
accroche: Some 12,000 courts tried nearly 1.2 million cases after the 1994 genocide. The name is old; the institution is new.
contenu_vulgarise:
In January 1998, Rwandan Vice President Paul Kagame announces that the country can no longer afford the $20 million a year its prison population costs. Four years after the 1994 genocide, some 130,000 prisoners are crammed into facilities built for 12,000, and detention conditions kill thousands. Ordinary courts have been trying genocide cases since December 1996, but by early 1998 only 1,292 people had been tried in all. At that rate, Human Rights Watch notes, the trials would have taken more than a century.

The government rejects proposals to bring in foreign judges and other judicial personnel. It proposes turning to an institution presented as customary, the *gacaca*, from the Kinyarwanda word for “grass”: the place where a community gathers to settle its disputes.

## What the Custom Was

According to HRW, little documentation exists on gacaca before 1994. The practice is thought to have emerged in precolonial times. Respected elders, the *inyangamugayo* (“those who detest disgrace”), mediated family and neighborhood conflicts there: property, inheritance, injuries, married life. More serious matters, such as cattle theft or murder, were left to chiefs or the king's representative.

## What It Became

The gacaca used after the genocide differs from this model on five points, according to HRW. It tries the most serious crimes, not minor disputes. It is fundamentally punitive (except for property offenses), with sentences that can go up to “life imprisonment with special provisions.” It depends on a state body, the National Service of Gacaca Courts, under the Ministry of Justice. It applies codified law, not customary law. And its judges are not elders but elected members of the community (HRW also calls them *inyangamugayo*), often fairly young, with a large share of women.

The 2001 law gives these courts jurisdiction over crimes committed between October 1, 1990 and December 31, 1994, for all suspects except those in category 1, whose cases remain before the ordinary courts. The new form is launched in June 2002, in twelve pilot sectors. According to HRW in 2011, a little over 12,000 courts have tried, since 2005, about 1.2 million cases. The figure remains uncertain: the service had announced between one million and 1.5 million cases and recorded 1,237,356 files, after detecting multiple entries in its database.

## What This Shifts

The government presented its choice as a return to “our traditional methods of conflict resolution.” HRW responds that, apart from the name and a few general traits, the version used for genocide cases “bears little resemblance” to the customary form. President Kagame described it as an “African solution to African problems.” The starting point, meanwhile, was a count of 1,292 people tried against 130,000 detainees.

HRW's 2011 assessment is a “mixed legacy.” Some Rwandans praise the courts' speed and the involvement of communities. Government officials had warned that the judges, often without formal education or training, would struggle to apply the law correctly, that there was a risk of bias, and that the proceedings would not meet Rwanda's international fair-trial obligations. For the NGO, nearly ten years after the process began, many of these fears have proven well founded. The gacaca also tried no crimes committed by the Rwandan Patriotic Front.

HRW, which has monitored more than 350 gacaca cases since their creation, titled its report “Justice Compromised.”

repere.texte: According to Human Rights Watch, around 1998 Rwanda held about 130,000 prisoners in facilities built for 12,000, while, by early 1998, the ordinary courts had tried only 1,292 people in all: at that rate, the trials would have taken more than a century.
repere.source: Human Rights Watch, Justice Compromised: The Legacy of Rwanda's Community-Based Gacaca Courts, 2011

carte.punch: An ancient name, a new institution: the gacaca tried nearly 1.2 million cases.
carte.idee: In 1998, Rwanda holds 130,000 detainees and, by early 1998, had tried only 1,292 people. It then creates gacaca courts: about 12,000 of them, with elected judges, written law, and a state service. The name comes from a mediation by elders; the institution is a criminal court.

quiz.question: Why does HRW judge that the 2001 gacaca bear little resemblance to the customary form, despite the name?
choix: Because they are still presided over by elders, but now judge in writing
Because they no longer impose any prison sentences, only reconciliation
Because they were created by local chiefs, with no link to the Ministry of Justice
Because they try serious crimes, punish, answer to a state service, and have elected judges
quiz.explication: According to HRW, customary gacaca had elders mediate family or neighborhood disputes. The 2001 version tries the most serious crimes, punishes (up to life imprisonment), depends on a Ministry of Justice service, applies codified law, and has elected judges. The other three answers describe the opposite of what the report finds.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the Rwandan government announce in January 1998 that the judicial system must change?
choix: Because the ordinary courts had already tried all the genocide cases
Because foreign judges refused to come work in Rwanda
Because it can no longer pay the annual cost of its prisons, while only 1,292 people have been tried
Because gacaca already existed as criminal courts before 1994
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Human Rights Watch reports that Rwanda could no longer pay the $20 million a year its prison population cost, with only 1,292 people tried in 1998.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the 2001 law set the jurisdiction of the gacaca courts?
choix: They try crimes committed between October 1, 1990 and December 31, 1994, except category 1
They try all crimes committed since Rwanda's independence in 1962
They try only category 1 crimes, the most serious
They try crimes committed after the national service was set up in 2002
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2001 law gives the gacaca jurisdiction over crimes from October 1, 1990 to December 31, 1994, for all suspects except category 1, which remained before the ordinary courts.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Human Rights Watch, which perpetrators did the gacaca never try?
choix: Crimes committed by the Rwandan Patriotic Front
quiz_supplementaire.explication: HRW notes that the gacaca tried genocide, categories 2 and 3, and handed down sentences up to life imprisonment, but prosecuted no crimes by the Rwandan Patriotic Front.
